data.text/markdown:
Classic signals · steps 1 to 4: the indicators, the trading rules, the levels

This is the workbench of a new strategy for ServiceNow (NOW), GE Vernova (GEV) and Rigetti Computing (RGTI): Bollinger Bands, moving averages, the trend of each stock's sector and of the market, and major price levels, each one a switch that can be turned on or off. Step 1 trades nothing. It shows the data and every indicator, so you can check that they look right before any rule relies on them:
  1. Data check: are all the one-minute candles there?
  2. The daily picture: candles, moving averages, major levels, report days, and the trend of the stock, its sector fund and the market fund
  3. Minute by minute: a few sessions with the bands, the moving average, the levels, the sector and the market, the typical move and the volume
  4. Band behaviour: how often the price closes outside its bands
Step 2 trades, with the first rules as switches:
  1. The first trading rules: two band triggers (fade and breakout), the sector-trend filter and the trailing stop, and what each switch says candle by candle
  2. Results by market condition (up, sideways, down) and by side (long, short), the profit curve and the bottom line (profit ÷ worst drawdown)
  3. Every trade, and why: click a trade to see it drawn and explained in words
Step 3 adds three more filters as switches (the minute chart's moving average, the stock's own daily trend and the market's daily trend) and:
  1. What each switch changes: every rule switched off and on, everything else as set, and where the difference comes from (market condition, half-year)
Step 4 adds the levels: two filters that keep a trade from running straight into a major level or the previous session's high or low (sections 5 and 8), and an optional profit target at the next level (under "The exit"). Rigetti joins as a third stock, with QTUM (a quantum-computing fund) as its sector. Step 5 adds the earnings guard (a switch: no trade held through a quarterly report) and:
  1. Tuning with a moving window: Optuna re-tunes the numbers of each stock every few sessions on the sessions just before, and the next sessions trade with the winner; windows of 20, 40, 60, 120 and all sessions before, against no tuning at all
The sliders change every chart at once. The final-check months (July to October 2026) are only counted in the data check, never drawn or traded: they stay untouched until the very end.

data.text/html: The notebook reads its helper files (data.py, rules/, …) once; this button reads them again and reruns everything, without restarting the kernel.

data.text/markdown:
Settings

The stocks, the fund that stands for each one's sector, the market fund, and the periods. The sector funds: IGV (software) for ServiceNow, XLI (industrials) for GE Vernova, and QTUM (the Defiance Quantum ETF, about 70 quantum-computing and machine-learning companies) for Rigetti. QTUM holds Rigetti at only about 2%, so its trend is the theme's, not Rigetti's own.
  • EXPLORE: the months every chart and (later) every test uses
  • FINAL_CHECK: kept aside for one honest look at the very end; here only counted
  • DAILY_FROM: daily candles start a year earlier, so a 50-day trend and the major levels are ready on the first day of EXPLORE

1 · Data check

How many one-minute candles each symbol has on each session, from the first day of EXPLORE to the last day of FINAL_CHECK (counted in the database, no prices loaded). A regular session has 390 candles (09:30 to 16:00); a half-day has 210 (the market closes at 13:00, e.g. the day after Thanksgiving). Two things to know about ServiceNow:
  • Minutes without a trade: candles where nobody traded; Interactive Brokers then repeats the last price with zero volume. ServiceNow has many of them in 2025 (up to 18% of the minutes in June 2025, mostly around midday) and none since January 2026: before its 5-for-1 split in December 2025 one share cost about $1,000, so fewer shares changed hands each minute. The prices here are split-adjusted throughout
  • Half-days: its stored candles continue after the 13:00 close on the three half-days (after-hours trades labelled as regular hours). They are counted as after-hours ("half-day candles after 13:00")
The pre-market (04:00-09:30, up to 330 minutes), after-hours (16:00-20:00, up to 240 minutes) and overnight (20:00-04:00, up to 480 minutes; only special venues trade then, Sunday to Thursday nights) columns give the typical number of stored minutes per session and the share of them with an actual trade. Outside regular hours far fewer shares change hands, so many minutes have no trade at all. Nothing trades on Saturday and Sunday daytime.

data.text/markdown:
Loading the candles

The one-minute candles of all five symbols for EXPLORE, the regular session (09:30-16:00) AND every hour around it: pre-market (04:00-09:30), after-hours (16:00-20:00) and overnight (20:00-04:00, where stored), and the daily candles from DAILY_FROM. The strategy will only trade in the regular session; the other hours are read as information. Table 2 compares each day's last regular-session close with the stored daily close: they should be within a few hundredths of a percent (the official close comes from the closing auction a moment after 15:59). A large gap would mean the two disagree about a split or a dividend.

data.text/markdown:
The indicator settings

Every slider redraws the charts below. These are the starting values of the strategy's knobs; later, the optimizer will tune them.
  • Bollinger Bands: an average of the last closes with a band above and below, a set number of standard deviations away. The bands widen when prices swing and narrow when they calm down
  • Moving average: an average of the last closes, drawn on the minute chart. The moving average filter (step 3) only trades in the direction it is going
  • The switch "bands and average also read the hours outside the regular session": off, both read the regular session only (09:30-16:00), and the hours before the open enter as their own numbers (Figure 4c); on, both run through every stored minute, pre-market, after-hours and overnight included. They react earlier then, but the thin trading outside regular hours makes them jumpier
  • Daily trend: up when the close is above its average and the average is rising; down when below and falling; sideways otherwise. "Flat" means the average moved less than a fraction of a typical day's move (Figure 2b shows it day by day)
  • Major levels: prices where the daily chart turned (a high or low that stands out from the days around it) several times (Figure 2a shows how they are built)
  • Typical move: how far a candle typically moves (average true range). The trailing stop will be measured in it

data.text/markdown:
2 · The daily picture

Figure 2, top: one stock's daily candles with a 20-day and the trend's moving average, and the material of the major levels:
  • turning points (black triangles): a day whose high is the highest of the days around it (a swing high, ▼ above the candle) or whose low is the lowest (a swing low, ▲ below it)
  • major levels (short black dashes, one on every day the level was known): prices where several turning points line up. A long row of dashes is a level that held for months; a thicker dash has more turning points behind it. Figure 2a shows, for one day, exactly which turning points make which level
  • report days (pink dotted lines)
Figure 2, bottom: the three colored trend ribbons, explained right under the figure and day by day in Figure 2b. Figure 3 counts how many days were up, sideways or down.

symbols: the stock
(NOW), its sector fund (IGV) and the market fund (SPY). Each day is judged at its
own close, by the same rule for all three:</span>
<ul>
<li><strong>blue, up</strong>: the close is above its 50-day average, AND that average
  rose over the last 10 days by more than 0.5 typical daily
  moves</li>
<li><strong>red, down</strong>: the close is below its 50-day average, AND that average
  fell by more than 0.5 typical daily moves</li>
<li><strong>gray, sideways</strong>: everything else: the average barely moved, or the price and the
  average disagree (the price below a rising average, or above a falling one)</li>
</ul>
<span class="paragraph">A "typical daily move" is the average size of the last 14 daily candles, gaps included, so
the rule is equally strict for a calm fund and a jumpy stock. The strategy will act on a
day's trend from the NEXT session on, since that close is not known during the day. The
sliders under "Daily trend" change it; <strong>Figure 2b</strong> shows the calculation day by day.</span></span></div>

data.text/markdown:
How the major levels are built (Figure 2a)

Pick a day. Figure 2a zooms into the sessions before it and shows how the levels known at its open come about, in three steps, each with its own lever:
  1. Find the turning points. A day is a swing high when its high is the highest of the days on both sides of it (lever: turning point: highest/lowest of ± days), a swing low when its low is the lowest. A turning point only counts once those days after it have passed: before that, nobody could know the price would not go further. More days = fewer, more important turning points
  2. Keep the recent ones. Only turning points from the last memory sessions count. A longer memory brings in older levels
  3. Group the ones that line up. Turning points whose prices are closer than the grouping distance count as the same level (lever: same level if closer than, in typical daily moves; a typical daily move is the average size of the last 14 daily candles, overnight gaps included, and the price amount is printed under the figure). A group with at least turning points needed members is a major level, at the average price of its turning points. A wider distance merges more points into fewer, broader levels; more turning points needed keeps only the strongest
The switch a ceiling and a floor may form one level decides whether swing highs and swing lows group together. On: a price where the stock turned up (a floor) and later turned down (a ceiling) is one level, since an old floor that breaks often becomes a ceiling. Off: swing highs make only ceiling (resistance) levels and swing lows only floor (support) levels. A point joins a group when it is within the grouping distance of its nearest neighbour in it, so a level of several points can be a little wider than the distance itself. Black triangles belong to a major level, hollow gray ones do not. Hover a triangle: it says from which session on the strategy may use it, and why it is (or is not) part of a level. The gray zone around each dashed level spans its turning points plus half the grouping distance on each side. The four levers below are the same as in the settings panel: moving one moves both.

How the trend is judged (Figure 2b)

Pick the stock, its sector fund or the market fund. Figure 2b shows the rule at work, day by day, in three panels:
  1. the daily close, one dot per day colored by the result (blue up, gray sideways, red down), and the trend average. Hover a dot: it says why, in words
  2. how much the average rose or fell over the last days, against the gray flat zone: above the zone the average counts as rising, below it as falling, inside it as flat
  3. the resulting ribbon, the same as under Figure 2
The three levers below are the same as in the settings panel.

3 · Minute by minute

Pick a first session and how many to show. Figure 4 has five panels on one time axis (nights and weekends are cut out):
  1. Candles with the Bollinger Bands (gray, shaded between), the moving average (amber), the major levels known at each session's open (black dashes) and the previous session's high and low (gray dots). Candles outside regular hours are pale (choose which hours to show: regular only, 04:00-20:00, or all 24); dotted lines mark the regular open (09:30) and close; the pre-market's high and low (gray dash-dots) run across the regular session
  2. Where the close sits in the band: 0 on the lower band, 1 on the upper band; dots mark the closes outside the band, the moments a band signal will look at
  3. The stock against its sector and the market, in percent since the first candle
  4. The typical move: how far the price typically travels within one candle of the size set under "Typical move" (15 minutes by default: its high minus its low, averaged over the last 14 such candles), in percent of the price. The trailing stop will keep a multiple of it behind the price. Figure 4b shows how it is computed
  5. Volume
Table 3 lists what was known at each session's open, the night before it included.

data.text/markdown:
What the typical move is (Figure 4b)

The typical move says how far the price normally travels in a short while, so that a stop can be set wide enough not to be hit by ordinary noise, and no wider. It is computed from candles of a fixed size (lever: candle size, 15 minutes by default) in three steps:
  1. Each candle's move: its high minus its low. If the previous candle closed outside that range, the move is stretched to reach it (this is called the "true range"). The jump over the night is left out, so one gap at the open does not inflate the whole morning
  2. Average the last few: the typical move is the average of the last candles averaged moves (14 by default). It only uses candles that have closed: while a candle runs, its own move is not known yet
  3. In percent of the price, so a $100 and a $1,000 stock compare
Figure 4b shows the sessions of Figure 4 on candles of that size: the gray bars are each candle's move, the green line is the typical move the strategy knows while the candle runs. A bar above the line is a candle that moved more than usual. The trailing stop (step 2) will sit a multiple of the line behind the best price: with a typical move of 0.5%, a stop of 3 typical moves trails 1.5% behind.

data.text/markdown:
The hours before the open (Figure 4c)

Everything that happens between the previous session's close (16:00) and the next open (09:30): the after-hours, the overnight (where stored) and the pre-market, summed up per session. All of it is known at 09:30, before the strategy may trade:
  • move before the open: from the previous close to the last trade before 09:30, in percent
  • pre-market high and low: the highest and lowest trade from 04:00 to 09:30 (drawn in Figure 4 as gray dash-dots across the regular session); the night's own high and low (since the previous close) are kept too
  • volume against its usual level: the shares traded between the close and the open, divided by their average over the previous 20 sessions. 1 is a usual night, 3 means three times as busy, which often comes with news
Only minutes with a trade count: a minute without one just repeats an older price. Figure 4c shows these numbers for every session of EXPLORE; Table 3b how big they typically are.

4 · Band behaviour

Over every regular-hours candle of EXPLORE (where the strategy trades): where the close sits in its band (Figure 5), and how often it closes outside (Table 4). The share outside the bands is how often a band signal can even start; wider bands make it rarer.

data.text/html: Table 4 · How often the close is outside the band

data.text/markdown:
5 · The trading rules (steps 2 and 3)

From here on the strategy trades: in the regular session only (09:30-16:00), each stock on its own, one trade at a time, long or short. Every rule is a switch. The three filters added in step 3 (moving average, stock trend, market trend) start switched off, so the default is still step 2's strategy; section 8 shows what each one changes. Triggers propose a trade at a candle's close:
  • band fade: the close comes back inside the bands after a close outside them: long when it climbs back above the lower band, short when it falls back below the upper band. The bet: the stretch snaps back
  • band breakout: the close stays outside the bands for a set number of candles in a row (lever closes in a row outside the band, 2 by default): long above the upper band, short below the lower band. One close outside alone may still turn straight back inside, which is the fade's case; the breakout fires once per stretch, at the close of its n-th candle. The bet: the move carries on
Filters allow or block a side. The four trend filters share one rule: up allows longs only, down shorts only, sideways (or not known yet) both:
  • moving average (step 3): the trend of the minute chart's moving average (the amber line of Figure 4), judged at each candle's close: up when the close is above the average AND the average rose over the last candles (lever) by more than a flat zone (lever, in typical moves); down when below a falling average; sideways otherwise
  • stock trend (step 3): the stock's own daily trend (Figure 2b), judged at the previous session's close. It is also the market condition every result is split by
  • sector trend: the same daily rule on the sector fund (IGV for NOW, XLI for GEV, QTUM for RGTI)
  • market trend (step 3): the same daily rule on the market fund (SPY)
  • major levels (step 4): no long while the nearest major level above the close (the levels of Figure 2a, known at the open) is closer than a set room (lever, in typical moves: 2 by default), no short while the nearest one below is; a level right at the close blocks both
  • previous high / low (step 4): the same rule on the previous session's high and low (whichever is above the price is a ceiling, whichever is below a floor)
  • wait after the open: no new trade in the first minutes after 09:30 (lever, 15 by default): a signal whose trade would fill in that time is dropped. Trades already open keep their stop
  • earnings guard (step 5, on by default): no new trade in the session(s) before a quarterly report's reaction day (the first session that can move on it: the same day for a report before the open, the next for one after the close), and an open trade is closed at the close before it. A report can move a stock 10% or more over a night
How they decide together. At every candle's close the switched-on triggers propose. If two of them propose opposite sides, the signal is not clear and nothing happens. A proposed side also needs every switched-on filter to allow it. The trade is then bought (long) or sold short at the NEXT candle's open, in the same session: a signal on a session's last candle is dropped, since the next open comes after a night. While a trade is open, new signals are ignored. How a trade ends: the trailing stop. It starts a set number of typical moves (Figure 4b) away from the entry price. After every candle it moves up to the same distance below the highest price since the entry (for a long; above the lowest price for a short), and never back. A candle that trades through it closes the trade at the stop price. A candle that OPENS beyond it (after a night, or a jump) closes the trade at that open, which is the real loss. Optionally, a holding limit closes the trade at the close of its n-th session. The profit target (step 4, optional, under "The exit"): the next level in the trade's direction, at least one typical move from the entry, fixed when the trade opens: the next major level, or the next major level or previous session's high or low. A candle that reaches it closes the trade there; one that opens beyond it fills at that better open. If the stop and the target fall in the same candle, the stop counts (the cautious reading). The market condition of a trade is the stock's own daily trend at the entry (judged at the previous close): up, sideways or down. The strategy is meant to hold up in all three.

data.text/html:
The rules (a new rule is one new file in rules/; its switch and its levers appear here)
trigger: A close outside a band, then a close back inside: long when it comes back from below the lower band, short when it comes back from above the upper band.
trigger: The close stays outside a band for a set number of candles in a row: long above the upper band, short below the lower band.
filter: The minute chart's moving average: above a rising average allows longs only, below a falling one shorts only, a flat one both.
filter: The stock's own daily trend at the previous close: up allows longs only, down shorts only, sideways both.
filter: The sector fund's daily trend at the previous close: up allows longs only, down shorts only, sideways both.
filter: The market fund's (SPY) daily trend at the previous close: up allows longs only, down shorts only, sideways both.
filter: No long just under a major level and no short just above one: the next level must leave some room (in typical moves).
filter: No long just under the previous session's high or low, no short just above one: it must leave some room (in typical moves).
filter: No new trade in the first minutes after 09:30: a signal whose trade would fill in that time is dropped (open trades keep their stop).
filter: No new trade in the session(s) before a quarterly report moves the stock, and an open trade is closed at the close before it.
The exit

Bollinger Bands (band fade, band breakout)
Moving average (the moving average filter)
Daily trend (stock, sector and market trend)
Typical move (the trailing stop, the moving average's flat zone)

Costs (the repo's cost model, config/settings.yaml): ||(10,000** per trade. Commission **||)0.005 a share, at least $1.00 an order (a stock above $50 pays the minimum; Rigetti at $10 is 1,000 shares, $5 an order). Every fill loses 0.02% of the price (half the bid-ask spread plus slippage), but at least half a cent a share: half the smallest possible spread of one cent, which is more than 0.02% below $25 a share. The table shows what a round trip costs at each stock's typical price: a trade must move more than that before it makes money.

The sessions picked below, regular hours only. Top: the candles, the Bollinger Bands, the moving average (amber), the trailing stop of an open trade (black dots, one step per candle) and the trades (blue ▲ a long entry, orange ▼ a short entry, ✕ the exit; hover a marker for the result). Bottom: one row per rule, then the decision and whether a trade is open. Hover a cell for its meaning:
  • a trigger row: blue = proposes long, orange = proposes short
  • a filter row: light gray = both sides allowed, blue = longs only, orange = shorts only, dark gray = neither side
  • decision: blue / orange = a long / short signal (filled at the next candle's open); dark gray = a proposal that a filter blocked, or two triggers that disagreed
  • in a trade: blue = long, orange = short
A switched-off rule keeps its row, marked "off": it shows what it would have said, but it takes no part in the decision. A signal while a trade is open is ignored.

6 · Results by market condition and side

Every trade of EXPLORE, every stock, after costs. Figure 7 shows the average result per trade by the market condition at the entry (the stock's own daily trend) and by side; the label on each bar is the number of trades. A strategy that works in every market has bars above zero in all three conditions. Table 5 gives the details, Table 5b splits the same trades by setup (the trigger that fired). The columns: winners is the share of trades that made money; average and median return % are per trade, in percent of the $10,000; the profit factor is the dollars won divided by the dollars lost (above 1: more won than lost); sessions held counts the entry's own session as 1.

data.text/markdown:
The profit curve and the bottom line (Figure 8, Table 6)

Figure 8: the profit in dollars, added up trade after trade (a step at every exit), per stock and for all together; below it, how far the total is under its best level so far (the drawdown). Table 6 holds the number the optimizer will judge later (step 5), for each stock on its own: the total profit divided by the worst drawdown. 2 means the strategy made twice as much as it ever gave back from a peak. For reference, the same numbers for simply buying $10,000 of the stock on the first day and holding it to the last. The strategy's drawdown is read at every exit, holding's at every session's close: a loss inside an open trade only counts once the trade has closed.

7 · Every trade, and why (Table 7, Figure 9)

Table 7 lists every trade; search, sort and filter it in the table. Click a row: Figure 9 draws that trade from an hour of candles before its signal to half an hour after its exit, with the bands, the trailing stop as it moved, the signal, the entry and the exit. The text under it tells the trade's story: which trigger fired and why, what each filter said, where the stop started and why the trade ended. Without a click it shows the first trade.

8 · What each switch changes (step 3)

For every rule, the whole strategy runs twice: once with that rule switched off and once with it switched on, every other switch, lever and setting as set above.
  • Figure 10: one line per rule, per stock and for all together. The hollow circle is the total profit after costs with the rule off, the filled one with it on (blue when switching it on made more, red when less). The label says how the rule is set now. Hover for the trades and profit ÷ worst drawdown
  • Figure 11: where that change comes from. Each cell is the change in profit from switching the rule on, within one market condition (the stock's own daily trend at the entry) or one half-year (by the exit). An empty cell had no trade either way
  • Table 8: the numbers
How to read it. Step 2 showed that the total moves by several thousand dollars with small changes of any lever, by chance alone. So read a switch as helpful only if it helps in most cells of Figure 11, for every stock: in each market condition and in each half-year, not only in the total.
